sources.sample: 28 primary schools in deprived areas; 1,213 Year 5 children aged 9–10.
sources.endpoint: Cycle helmet ownership and wearing.
sources.finding: The pack arm was not statistically distinguishable from the multifaceted arm for ownership (reported OR 1.51, 95% CI 0.50–4.58) or wearing (OR 0.98, 0.57–1.68). Ownership increased from baseline in both arms; the pack arm also had a significant baseline-to-follow-up increase in wearing. Authors report reduced inequality in helmet ownership.
sources.limits: Both arms included access to a free helmet; not leaflet-only versus no intervention. Wide CIs do not demonstrate equivalence. Outcomes were ownership and wearing, not crashes or injuries.
sources.access: Open full-text trial

sources.authors: Department for Transport / THINK!
sources.title: THINK! Cycling Evaluation 2016: Don’t get caught campaign
sources.design: Pre/post cyclist surveys; no randomized control
sources.sample: 573 pre; 500 post
sources.endpoint: Recall, self-report, blame and participation intentions
sources.finding: Some respondents perceived rider blame or anticipated cycling less.
sources.limits: Survey reactions are not observed riding or causal injury effects.
sources.access: Original official evaluation PDF

sources.authors: DiMaggio, C.; Brady, J.; Li, G.
sources.title: Association of the Safe Routes to School program with school-age pedestrian and bicyclist injury risk in Texas
sources.design: Observational program evaluation with adult trend comparison
sources.sample: Texas statewide injury series
sources.endpoint: Combined pedestrian/bicyclist injuries
sources.finding: Decline associated with program period; causal attribution unresolved.
sources.limits: Pre-existing decline and secular trends; combined mode endpoint; not education-only.
sources.access: Open full article

sources.authors: Box, E.
sources.title: Highway Code Intervention Evaluation Report
sources.design: Randomized three-arm online pre/post/follow-up evaluation of the Co-Pilot Highway Code film against two road-safety film controls. The film covered updated rules for different road users; measured cycling-specific knowledge included overtaking distance, while the measured turning-priority question concerned a pedestrian waiting to cross as a driver turns into a side road.
sources.sample: pre post: 254; follow up: 210; population: licensed UK drivers age 25+; unit: survey participants
sources.endpoint: Highway Code knowledge, including pedestrian turning priority and cyclist passing distance; self-reported intentions, perceived control and norms.
sources.finding: Correct responses to the pedestrian-priority rule for a driver turning into a side road rose in the intervention group from 67% at baseline to 99% immediately and 87% at 4-6 weeks. Correct responses to the cyclist overtaking-distance item rose from 37% to 73% and were 51% at follow-up. Group-by-time analyses favored the intervention over controls. Self-reported intentions, perceived behavioral control, and social norms also showed group-by-time signals.
sources.limits: Questionnaire knowledge and self-reported behavioral determinants, not observed driving or passing; the turning knowledge item was about pedestrian priority, not cyclist priority; online Prolific sample; short follow-up; the evaluation was self-funded by Co-Pilot, the intervention developer; no crash endpoint.
sources.access: Full report

sources.authors: Hess, G.; Peterson, M. N.
sources.title: Bicycles May Use Full Lane Signage Communicates U.S. Roadway Rules and Increases Perception of Safety
sources.design: Web-based randomized scenario survey assigning respondents to BMUFL, Share the Road, shared-lane markings, or unsigned-roadway conditions; outcomes were rule comprehension and perceived safety.
sources.sample: responses received: 1978; analyzed: 1824; unit: U.S. survey respondents
sources.endpoint: Correct recognition of bicycle lane-use and passing rules and perceived safety in hypothetical road scenarios.
sources.finding: BMUFL improved correct recognition of lane-use and passing rules in most scenarios and increased perceived safety. Share the Road responses did not differ significantly from unsigned-roadway responses. No road behavior or crash outcome was measured.
sources.limits: Twitter-recruited convenience sample; hypothetical image scenarios; responses measure understanding and perception rather than actual behavior; some reported comparisons use p<.10.
sources.access: Full peer-reviewed open-access article

sources.authors: Lahrmann, H.; Madsen, T. K. O.; Olesen, A. V.; Madsen, J. C. O.; Hels, T.
sources.title: The effect of a yellow bicycle jacket on cyclist accidents
sources.design: One-year randomized trial of yellow high-visibility jacket versus regular clothing, using monthly self-reported accidents; corrected rates account for apparent differential under-reporting.
sources.sample: 6,793 volunteer Danish adult cyclists: 3,402 test and 3,391 control; regular cyclists riding at least three times per week in summer.
sources.endpoint: Monthly self-reported bicycle accidents, including multiparty personal-injury accidents; reported jacket use.
sources.finding: For multiparty personal-injury accidents more severe than bruising, uncorrected accident-rate ratio (ARR) 0.53 (95% CI 0.37–0.77). After correction for apparent reporting bias, ARR 0.62 (0.39–1.00), marked significant by the paper. Average reported jacket use was about 77%.
sources.limits: Unblinded, volunteer and frequent adult Danish cyclists; monthly self-report. Correction assumes single-party injury reports indicate reporting bias for multiparty events; estimate is equipment efficacy, not campaign/message effect.
sources.access: Open full-text author/institutional PDF and publisher article page

sources.authors: Pless, I. B.; Verreault, R.; Tenina, S.
sources.title: A case-control study of pedestrian and bicyclist injuries in childhood
sources.design: Montreal hospital case-control study; blinded parent interviews and tests; logistic regression adjusted for age, gender, and socioeconomic area.
sources.sample: 200 traffic-injured children aged 0–14 (MAIS score at least 2) and 400 uninjured hospital controls; pedestrians and bicyclists combined.
sources.endpoint: Traffic injury among child pedestrians and bicyclists in relation to parental supervision and other risk factors.
sources.finding: Poor parental supervision was associated with injury; the study reports OR 2.6 (95% CI 1.5–4.7) for poor versus good supervision. It also identifies parental education, family accident history, and unsafe environment as relevant associations.
sources.limits: Mixed pedestrian/cyclist outcome, observational design, hospital controls, and no tested supervision message or intervention. Does not establish an age threshold for independent cycling or prove supervision alone prevents injury.
sources.access: Open full-text article; exact estimate also indexed in article text

sources.authors: Nawaz, I.; Cuenen, A.; Ahmed, T.; Zeb, A.; Wets, G.; Janssens, D.
sources.title: Road Safety education for children and adolescents: A systematic review of effectiveness, methods, and challenges
sources.design: PRISMA-described systematic review searching Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science; studies published 2004–2024 across multiple road-user types and education formats.
sources.sample: 46 studies across 26 countries; the publisher abstract does not give a participant total or cyclist-only subgroup size.
sources.endpoint: Reported changes in road-safety knowledge, attitudes and behavior in included education studies.
sources.finding: The authors report that 83% of studies found significant knowledge improvement, 71% positive attitude changes, and 68% measurable behavior improvement. The outcomes included pedestrian and cycling behaviors; the abstract does not provide pooled effect sizes or a bicycle-specific crash/injury estimate.
sources.limits: Percentages count studies with reported positive findings; they are not pooled effect sizes or proportions of children helped. Broad road-safety scope, heterogeneous methods, and no cyclist-specific injury conclusion in the accessible abstract. Full text not accessed.
sources.access: Publisher article page and abstract; full text paywalled/not accessed

sources.authors: Ipsos UK
sources.title: An evaluation of the ADI Cycle Awareness Pilot
sources.design: Randomized delayed-access trial of online cycle-awareness training for approved driving instructors; learner-driver access was also offered but not completed.
sources.sample: recruited baseline: 2339; treatment baseline: 1169; control baseline: 1170; endline comparison: 629; endline treatment: 179; endline control: 450; learner drivers registered: 33; learner drivers completed: 0; unit: instructors and learner drivers
sources.endpoint: Instructor attitudes toward cyclists, awareness and perceptions, and self-reported driving and teaching intentions.
sources.finding: Only 2 of 13 cyclist-attitude items showed a statistically significant treatment effect: cyclist-as-nuisance was lower by 0.33 scale points; cyclist-fault-for-crashes was lower by 0.23, marginal after Bonferroni adjustment. Awareness of Bikeability increased. No driving behavior was measured.
sources.limits: Only 15% of recruited ADIs completed the learning and endline; severe attrition and unbalanced endline samples; no learner-driver completions; attitudes and intended teaching rather than observed driving; no crash endpoint.
sources.access: Full Ipsos UK report dated December 2022 and appendices; published by Department for Transport on GOV.UK on 31 October 2024

sources.authors: Kwan, I.; Mapstone, J.
sources.title: Interventions for increasing pedestrian and cyclist visibility for the prevention of death and injuries
sources.design: Cochrane systematic review of randomized visibility-aid trials; searches last updated May 2009.
sources.sample: 35 papers reporting 42 detection/recognition trials, 1,171 participants; no eligible crash/injury trials were found in the review search.
sources.endpoint: Driver detection and recognition tasks, plus cyclist/pedestrian collision and injury endpoints where available.
sources.finding: Some fluorescent materials improved daytime detection; lamps, flashing lights, and retroreflective materials improved detection or recognition at night. No trial measured crash or injury reduction at the time of the review.
sources.limits: Most outcomes were surrogate visibility tasks; only a subset directly involved cyclists; diverse interventions and settings prevented a pooled effect estimate. Search predates newer equipment trials.
sources.access: Open full review and Cochrane summary.

sources.authors: Madsen, J. C. O.; Andersen, T.; Lahrmann, H. S.
sources.title: Safety effects of permanent running lights for bicycles: A controlled experiment
sources.design: Controlled 12-month trial of bicycle-mounted permanent running lights; accident rates compared between a treatment and control group.
sources.sample: 3,845 cyclists in Odense, Denmark: 1,845 light-equipped treatment bicycles and 2,000 controls.
sources.endpoint: Self-reported bicycle accidents and personal injuries, including multiparty accidents, per person-month.
sources.finding: The authors report 19% lower incidence of all recorded self-reported bicycle accidents with personal injury in the light group, measured per person-month; abstract also reports a significant reduction in multiparty accidents.
sources.limits: Equipment trial, not a messaging intervention. Accident data self-reported online; report itself discusses potential reporting shortcomings. Person-month denominator is not distance cycled; no CI in accessible abstract; one Danish setting.
sources.access: Original full journal article PDF supplied by reader; indexed PubMed record.

sources.authors: Kay, J. J.; Savolainen, P. T.; Gates, T. J.; Datta, T. K.
sources.title: Driver behavior during bicycle passing maneuvers in response to a Share the Road sign treatment
sources.design: Before/after field study of passing behavior at two similar rural two-lane highway segments; observed vehicle lateral position and speed with and without the Share the Road sign treatment and in settings with/without centerline rumble strips.
sources.sample: Observed passing events on two rural two-lane road segments; see original article for model-specific samples.
sources.endpoint: Observed vehicle lateral position, passing speed, cyclist buffer distance and crowding probability.
sources.finding: The sign shifted vehicles away from rightmost lane positions and reduced passing speed by 2.5 mph (4.0 km/h); it did not significantly affect mean buffer distance or crowding probability. Centerline rumble strips tended to shift vehicles closer to cyclists, marginally.
sources.limits: Specific high-speed rural sites; field before/after design; no crash endpoint. Speed, lateral position, buffer distance and crowding are distinct outcomes.
sources.access: Full original journal PDF supplied by reader; abstract and field results checked

sources.authors: Sinclair, J.; Nolan, J.
sources.title: Do minimum passing distance laws for cyclists change driver behaviour?
sources.design: PassBox before/after instrumented passing-distance study in Perth following a minimum passing-distance law introduced alongside an advertising campaign.
sources.sample: cyclists: 70; unit: cyclists; passing-event count not stated in the accessible abstract
sources.endpoint: Instrumented motor-vehicle passing distance before and after the combined law and advertising change.
sources.finding: For roads at or below 60 km/h, the closest 5% of passes were 10 cm farther from cyclists after the combined law/advertising change (95% CI 2-19 cm). No effect was observed on roads at or above 70 km/h.
sources.limits: Combined law/advertising change, not campaign-only; pre/post observation; closest 5% estimate rather than average. Local preprint reports 12 cm (4.9–19.0); published abstract reports 10 cm (2–19). Use published value.
sources.access: Local author preprint plus published journal abstract; published abstract used for the 10 cm estimate

sources.authors: Olivier, J.; Creighton, P.
sources.title: Bicycle injuries and helmet use: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.design: Systematic review and multivariate meta-regression of studies reporting medically diagnosed injury and known helmet use among cyclists involved in a crash or fall.
sources.sample: 43 eligible studies; 40 included in meta-analysis, with data from more than 64,000 injured cyclists.
sources.endpoint: Head, serious head, face, fatal head and neck injuries among cyclists involved in a crash or fall, by helmet use.
sources.finding: Helmet use associated with lower odds of head injury (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.42–0.57), serious head injury (0.31, 0.25–0.37), face injury (0.67, 0.56–0.81), and fatal head injury (0.35, 0.14–0.88). Neck injury association was unclear (0.96, 0.74–1.25).
sources.limits: Primarily observational injury studies and conditional on crash/fall involvement; estimates concern injury mitigation, not crash prevention or effect of a helmet campaign. Residual confounding remains possible.
sources.access: PubMed abstract and open full-text copy available from author/institutional sources

sources.authors: Carlin, J. B.; Taylor, P.; Nolan, T.
sources.title: School based bicycle safety education and bicycle injuries in children: a case-control study
sources.design: Population-based case-control evaluation of exposure to a school bicycle-safety course among injured and uninjured children.
sources.sample: 148 injury cases and 130 controls aged 9–14 years.
sources.endpoint: Child bicycle injury associated with exposure to a school bicycle-safety education course.
sources.finding: No evidence of a protective effect: OR 1.64 (95% CI 0.98–2.75). Among boys, OR 2.0 (95% CI 1.1–3.8). Authors hypothesized inadvertent risk-taking or inadequate supervision as possible explanations.
sources.limits: Observational association cannot show the course caused harm; potential confounding, selection, and differences in exposure. Historical program and setting limit current transfer. Authors' proposed mechanism was not tested.
sources.access: Open full-text article PDF and PubMed record

sources.authors: Lankarani, K. B.; Akbari, M.; Razzaghi, A.; Taghi Heydari, S.; Vali, M.; Tabrizi, R.; Sullman, M. J. M.
sources.title: Mass media campaigns to increase the use of bicycle helmets: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of mass-media campaigns aimed at bicycle helmet use; searches covered January 2000 to February 2022.
sources.sample: Eight eligible articles; participant totals and study-level designs are not reported in the accessible abstract.
sources.endpoint: Bicycle helmet use following mass-media campaigns in included studies.
sources.finding: Pooled helmet-use OR 3.77 (95% CI 1.16–12.20); I²=99.9% (heterogeneity p<0.001). Abstract reports pooled p<0.001, which is not readily consistent with the displayed CI under a conventional two-sided Wald calculation. The endpoint is helmet wearing, not injury.
sources.limits: Extreme heterogeneity and only eight articles make the pooled magnitude unstable; campaigns and comparison designs vary and may include other components. Do not use as a campaign forecast. Full article text not accessed for this review.
sources.access: Publisher/indexed abstract; full article paywalled/not accessed

sources.authors: Reymond, L.; Rérat, P.
sources.title: Blaming Cyclists, Invisibilising Drivers: How Motonormativity Shapes Swiss Media Collision Reports
sources.design: Content analysis of newspaper articles and coded headline/body sentences about cyclist–motorist collisions.
sources.sample: 204 articles from six French-language Swiss newspapers, published 2020–2024; 179 headlines and 311 body-text sentences coded.
sources.endpoint: Presence of an explicit agent, narrative focus, vehicle/person references, episodic/systemic framing, and language patterns.
sources.finding: Explicit agents appeared in 27% of headlines; cyclists were the focus of 83% of headlines; motorists appeared in 42% and were usually referred to as vehicles (82%); 93% of stories used an episodic frame.
sources.limits: Describes one language, country, and newspaper sample. Content analysis does not measure audience interpretation, causality, driver behavior, or campaign effectiveness.
sources.access: Open full article, tables, and data files at Findings.

sources.authors: Tannenbaum, M. B.; Hepler, J.; Zimmerman, R. S.; Saul, L.; Jacobs, S.; Wilson, K.; Albarracín, D.
sources.title: Appealing to fear: A meta-analysis of fear appeal effectiveness and theories
sources.design: Cross-domain meta-analysis of experimental fear appeals with comparison groups and attitude, intention, or behavior outcomes.
sources.sample: 127 papers, 248 independent samples, N=27,372.
sources.endpoint: Composite and separate attitudes, intentions, and behaviors across diverse health and safety topics.
sources.finding: Small positive mean composite effect, random-effects d=.29 (95% CI .22–.35). Efficacy statements and one-time rather than repeated behaviors moderated effectiveness.
sources.limits: Not a cyclist or road-safety campaign estimate; pooled outcomes and behaviors span many domains. It does not establish that graphic imagery helps or that a fear appeal is safe for every audience.
sources.access: Open full text at PubMed Central; publisher PDF also publicly available.

sources.authors: Michie, S.; van Stralen, M. M.; West, R.
sources.title: The behaviour change wheel: A new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions
sources.design: Framework synthesis and development
sources.sample: 19 frameworks identified
sources.endpoint: Intervention design framework
sources.finding: Capability, opportunity and motivation organize barrier diagnosis.
sources.limits: Not a cyclist intervention trial or an efficacy guarantee.
sources.access: Open full article

sources.authors: Rhodes, N.; Shulman, H. C.; McClaran, N.
sources.title: Changing norms: A meta-analytic integration of research on social norms appeals
sources.design: Meta-analysis of experimental social-norm manipulations with comparison groups.
sources.sample: 110 articles; sample totals vary across outcome sets.
sources.endpoint: Attitudes, perceived norms, intentions, and behavior across multiple topics and settings.
sources.finding: Small average effects with significant heterogeneity. Fixed-effect behavior estimates were d=.10 for descriptive appeals (k=59) and d=.34 for injunctive appeals (k=11).
sources.limits: Broad cross-domain evidence, not cycling or traffic passing; effects depend on design, population, message, and outcome. Do not use the averages to forecast a cyclist message.
sources.access: Author manuscript publicly available; publisher record available.

sources.authors: Haworth, N.; Delbosc, A.; Schramm, A.; Haslam, N.
sources.title: How might advertising campaigns rehumanize cyclists?
sources.design: ACT minimum-passing-distance poster survey experiment comparing four designs: photo versus graphic and front versus rear view; photo/graphic comparison was within-person, with photo presented first to all respondents.
sources.sample: 267 usable survey responses.
sources.endpoint: Dehumanization/humanization scale ratings, attitudes toward cyclists, clarity, memorability, and perceived effectiveness.
sources.finding: Photographs produced small changes on humanization/dehumanization ratings but no overall attitude improvement. There was no overall front/rear main effect, but drivers rated the front-view cyclist more positively than the rear-view cyclist; cyclists did not show this pattern. Graphic versions received higher clarity, memorability, and perceived-effectiveness ratings. No actual driving was measured.
sources.limits: Convenience online sample from one jurisdiction; fixed photo-first order; self-report ratings and one local passing-rule message; no measured recall, driver behavior, or crashes. Findings do not test AI-generated imagery.
sources.access: Local author preprint; published journal abstract and full ACT project report. Local preprint is not the final peer-reviewed article.

sources.authors: Owen, R.; Kendrick, D.; Mulvaney, C.; Coleman, T.; Royal, S.
sources.title: Non-legislative interventions for the promotion of cycle helmet wearing by children
sources.design: Cochrane systematic review of randomized and controlled before-after studies
sources.sample: 29 studies; 11 in observed-wearing pool
sources.endpoint: Observed helmet wearing; self-reported wearing/ownership
sources.finding: Observed wearing favored intervention; OR2.08 (95%CI1.29-3.34).
sources.limits: Heterogeneous mixed designs; observed-wearing RCT-only pool (3 studies) uncertain, OR0.99, CI0.18-5.63. Components not randomized; wearing, not injury.
sources.access: Open full review

sources.authors: Prabhakharan, P.; Bennett, J. M.; Hurden, A.; Crundall, D.
sources.title: The efficacy of hazard perception training and education: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of hazard-perception training across road-user groups
sources.sample: Cyclist subgroup: seven study samples from five papers; two retention checks at three weeks
sources.endpoint: Video-based hazard-perception skills; cyclist road behavior was not assessed
sources.finding: Cyclist pooled Hedges g 0.97 (95% CI 0.52–1.42), k=7; considerable heterogeneity I-squared 87.01%. Two studies found performance above pre-training at three weeks.
sources.limits: Varied skill tasks and training methods, substantial heterogeneity; cyclist findings concern video-based hazard performance, not everyday behavior or injuries; brief retention follow-up.
sources.access: Original full journal PDF supplied by reader; cyclist results in sections 3.6.1–3.6.2 checked

sources.authors: Blomberg, R. D.; Wright, T. J.; Van Houten, R.; Finstad, K.; Thomas, F. D.
sources.title: Evaluating High-Visibility Enforcement of Bicycle Passing Laws
sources.design: Two-city repeated before/after evaluation of high-visibility enforcement combined with city publicity; police used ultrasonic devices with staged riders and volunteer cyclists.
sources.sample: daytime passes: 38886; knoxville passes: 19527; grand rapids passes: 19359; unit: instrumented vehicle-bicycle passing events
sources.endpoint: Instrumented passing distances and proportions of passes below legal thresholds for staged and volunteer riders.
sources.finding: Grand Rapids volunteer passes under 5 ft fell from 26.01% to 18.17% at the last wave (p<.001). Knoxville staged passes under 3 ft fell from 4.98% to 3.11% (p=.017). Several volunteer subgroup changes were not significant. No crash outcome was measured.
sources.limits: Publicity and police enforcement were bundled; no untreated comparison city; before/after design; staged and volunteer riders differ; measurement activity itself may have reminded drivers of the campaign. Do not attribute effects to publicity or posters alone.
sources.access: Full government report and metadata page

sources.authors: Carey, R. N.; McDermott, D. T.; Sarma, K. M.
sources.title: The impact of threat appeals on fear arousal and driver behavior: A meta-analysis of experimental research 1990–2011
sources.design: Meta-analysis of experimental driver-message studies published 1990–2011.
sources.sample: 13 studies; 71 effects; total N=3,044. Fear was measured in four studies, n=619.
sources.endpoint: Self-reported fear arousal and pooled driving behavior/intention outcomes, including lab/simulator and self-report measures.
sources.finding: Threat appeals increased fear (r=.64, p<.01). The pooled driving outcome was not statistically significant (r=.03, p=.17; approximately 95% CI −.01 to .07).
sources.limits: High heterogeneity; not bicycle-message-specific; no actual cyclist passing or bicycle crash outcomes. Nonsignificance is not an equivalence finding. Graphic/shock imagery was not isolated.
sources.access: Open full text at PLOS ONE and PubMed Central.

sources.authors: Phillips, R. O.; Ulleberg, P.; Vaa, T.
sources.title: Meta-analysis of the effect of road safety campaigns on accidents
sources.design: Meta-analysis/meta-regression of campaign evaluations with crash outcomes.
sources.sample: 67 studies, 119 crash-effect estimates, 12 countries, 1975–2007.
sources.endpoint: Road crashes across varied road-safety topics and campaign packages.
sources.finding: Adjusted weighted average was about a 9% crash reduction (95% interval about 6%–12% fewer crashes). Personal communication and roadside media were associated with stronger effects in between-study analyses.
sources.limits: Not cyclist-only and not print-only; substantial heterogeneity. Delivery components were not randomized, and the authors caution against using one average to forecast a new campaign.
sources.access: Original full journal article PDF supplied by reader; PubMed record.

sources.authors: Saleem, T.; et al.
sources.title: Crash-based evaluation of the Watch for Me NC program
sources.design: Empirical-Bayes county before-after program evaluation
sources.sample: 29 treatment; 71 reference counties
sources.endpoint: Pedestrian and bicycle crashes analyzed separately
sources.finding: Bicycle conclusion inconclusive under alternative exposure models.
sources.limits: Messaging, enforcement and engineering not separated; pedestrian result not cyclist effect.
sources.access: Original full government-commissioned report

sources.authors: Richmond, S. A.; Zhang, Y. J.; Stover, A.; Howard, A.; Macarthur, C.
sources.title: Prevention of bicycle-related injuries in children and youth: a systematic review of bicycle skills training interventions
sources.design: Systematic review of 16 databases; included observational and experimental bicycle-skill and safety-education studies; quality assessed with Downs and Black criteria.
sources.sample: 25 studies involving children under 19; 16 measured knowledge and 13 behavior or attitudes.
sources.endpoint: Injury, knowledge, behavior and attitude outcomes in bicycle skills and safety-education studies.
sources.finding: Review found no clear evidence of injury reduction. Eight of 16 studies reported knowledge gains; five of 13 reported behavior or attitude improvement. No clear relationship between study quality and those improvements.
sources.limits: Heterogeneous interventions and designs; review reports study counts rather than a pooled injury effect. Sparse high-quality evidence; null does not prove all training is ineffective.
sources.access: Full original journal PDF supplied by reader; abstract and Results/Discussion checked

sources.authors: Skivington, K.; et al.
sources.title: A new framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions: update of Medical Research Council guidance
sources.design: Methods and guidance framework
sources.sample: Not an effectiveness sample
sources.endpoint: Evaluation design, context and program theory
sources.finding: Develop and evaluate interventions iteratively in context.
sources.limits: Guidance, not a cyclist messaging effect estimate.
sources.access: Open full methods article

sources.authors: Embree, T. E.; Romanow, N. T. R.; Djerboua, M. S.; Morgunov, N. J.; Bourdeaux, J. J.; Hagel, B. E.
sources.title: Risk Factors for Bicycling Injuries in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review
sources.design: Systematic review of comparative studies published 1990–May 2015; bicyclists younger than 20; risk of bias assessed with Newcastle-Ottawa scales.
sources.sample: 14 articles; heterogeneous populations, exposures and injury definitions.
sources.endpoint: Bicycle injuries and associated risk factors among children and adolescents.
sources.finding: Lower socioeconomic status, on-road riding, riding in rural versus urban areas, and sidewalk riding were associated with bicycle injury. The review found that bicycle safety education did not protect children against future injury in the included evidence. Motor-vehicle collision injuries were more severe.
sources.limits: Study heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis; study quality was affected by unclear group definitions and self-reported data. Observational risk associations do not establish causal effects of education.
sources.access: Full original journal PDF supplied by reader; abstract, results and discussion checked

sources.authors: Goddard, T.; Ralph, K.; Thigpen, C. G.; Iacobucci, E.
sources.title: Does news coverage of traffic crashes affect perceived blame and preferred solutions? Evidence from an experiment
sources.design: Random assignment to one of three versions of a hypothetical news article about a fatal pedestrian crash: pedestrian-focused, driver-focused, or thematic/systemic framing.
sources.sample: 999 U.S. participants.
sources.endpoint: Stated allocation of blame, preferred punishment, and support for road-safety solutions.
sources.finding: Driver-focused wording shifted average blame share toward the driver (50.2% to 65.5%) and away from the pedestrian (43.1% to 30.0%) relative to pedestrian-focused wording. The thematic frame increased stated support for pedestrian infrastructure.
sources.limits: One hypothetical pedestrian fatality and a news article, not a cyclist PSA or real crash; judgments and policy preferences were reported, not actual driving or policy behavior.
sources.access: Open-access full paper; DOI and publisher record available.

sources.authors: Hels, T.; Madsen, T. K. O.; Christensen, M. C.; Tallaksen, A. B.; Lahrmann, H.
sources.title: The effect on cyclist safety of daytime running lights
sources.design: One-year randomized controlled trial of continuous daytime-running-light use versus usual light routine, with monthly self-reported accident surveys.
sources.sample: 5,380 volunteers randomized; 3,592 submitted at least one monthly survey; 230 accidents reported.
sources.endpoint: Self-reported cyclist accidents per participant-month, including multi-party and personal-injury accidents.
sources.finding: After reporting-bias correction, all multi-party accidents had IRR .70 (95% CI .39–1.28) and multi-party personal-injury accidents IRR .75 (.23–2.47), neither significant. Multi-party accidents in darkness had IRR .29 (.10–.84), a significant subgroup result.
sources.limits: Voluntary convenience sample; incomplete monthly survey response and self-reported accidents; wide confidence intervals. The dark subgroup result may reflect better nighttime lighting in the test group. This tests equipment use, not a public message encouraging it.
sources.access: Open full peer-reviewed article and institutional record.

sources.authors: Keppner, V.; Krumpoch, S.; Kob, R.; Rappl, A.; Sieber, C. C.; Freiberger, E.; Siebentritt, H. M.
sources.title: Safer cycling in older age (SiFAr): effects of a multi-component cycle training. A randomized controlled trial
sources.design: Parallel-group randomized controlled trial of eight cycling-exercise sessions over three months versus active health-advice control; standardized practical cycling course assessed before/after and at 6–9 months.
sources.sample: 127 adults aged 65+ randomized; 96 analyzed for primary outcome (47 intervention, 49 active control), mean age 73.4 years; participants were e-bike beginners, self-reported unsteady, or returning after a longer break.
sources.endpoint: Errors on a standardized practical cycling course after training and at 6–9 months.
sources.finding: Adjusted intervention effect was B=−2.51 fewer course errors after intervention (95% CI −4.05 to −0.96) and B=−3.02 at 6–9 months (−4.91 to −1.14). A separate unadjusted long-term model reported B=−3.07; do not label that as the adjusted result.
sources.limits: Standardized course skill outcome, not road crashes or injuries; course assessor not blinded; selected older adults with self-perceived training needs; 31 randomized participants not in primary-outcome analysis.
sources.access: Open full-text randomized trial

sources.authors: World Health Organization
sources.title: Road Safety Mass Media Campaigns: A Toolkit
sources.design: Official WHO campaign-planning toolkit; publication year follows the original PDF and its suggested citation
sources.sample: Not a cycling trial
sources.endpoint: Campaign development and delivery
sources.finding: Use audience research, implementation planning and evaluation.
sources.limits: Toolkit experience spans other road-safety topics; not cyclist-specific effect.
sources.access: Full original WHO toolkit PDF; 2016 publication, website listing dated 2019

sources.authors: World Health Organization
sources.title: Cyclist safety: an information resource for decision-makers and practitioners
sources.design: Official practitioner resource
sources.sample: Not an intervention sample
sources.endpoint: Safe System and cyclist safety planning
sources.finding: Combine behavioral measures with safer systems.
sources.limits: Practice guidance; not independent evidence that a message works.
sources.access: Full original WHO practitioner-resource PDF; 2020 edition

sources.authors: Yadav, R.-P.; Kobayashi, M.
sources.title: A systematic review: effectiveness of mass media campaigns for reducing alcohol-impaired driving and alcohol-related crashes
sources.design: Systematic review with pooled injury/fatality analysis
sources.sample: 19 studies; 7 pooled
sources.endpoint: Alcohol-related injury/fatality crashes
sources.limits: Indirect for cycling; heterogeneous media/enforcement packages and before-after designs.
sources.access: Original open review and indexed abstract

sources.authors: Delhomme, P.; et al. (eds.)
sources.title: Manual for Designing, Implementing, and Evaluating Road Safety Communication Campaigns, Part II: Deliverable 3.2b
sources.design: European CAST project practical campaign-planning manual; guidance synthesis, not intervention evaluation
sources.sample: 146-page public final Part II manual
sources.endpoint: Campaign planning, pretesting, implementation, process/outcome/economic evaluation
sources.finding: Describes a six-step planning cycle and recommends audience research, pretesting for clarity/appropriateness/appeal, and evaluation planning before launch.
sources.limits: Guidance is not a controlled test of any cyclist message or an estimate of injury reduction.
sources.access: Official Vias-hosted full 146-page PDF, also supplied by reader.

sources.authors: Dunn, N.; Greatbatch, R.; Radlbeck, J.; La Rose, C.; Bravo Bueno, J.
sources.title: Evaluating Traffic Safety Campaigns: A Guide
sources.design: Practice guide and evaluation framework; BTSCRP Research Report 14
sources.sample: No intervention sample; guidance for state highway safety offices and other campaign evaluators
sources.endpoint: Campaign awareness/reach, knowledge, attitudes, intentions, behavior, and long-term safety outcomes
sources.finding: Sets out formative, process, outcome, and impact evaluation; recommends matching metrics and methods to campaign goals and combining surveys/media metrics with observed behavior, citation, or crash data when appropriate. Awareness and knowledge alone do not establish behavior change. (PDF pp. 12–14; report pp. 2–4)
sources.limits: Guidance, not an effectiveness trial or cyclist-specific evidence review; US state highway safety office focus. Cost estimates are ranges and require local adaptation.
sources.access: Official National Academies page and full report PDF; 152 pp.

sources.authors: Dunn, N.; Greatbatch, R.; Radlbeck, J.; La Rose, C.; Bravo Bueno, J.
sources.title: Objectives, Components, and Measures of Effective Traffic Safety Public Awareness and Education Efforts
sources.design: Conduct-of-research report documenting a phased literature/environmental scan and toolkit development
sources.sample: 40 sources: 21 peer-reviewed studies, 17 reports, one web page, and one book chapter; traffic safety campaigns mainly in the US
sources.endpoint: Evaluation methods and metrics used for campaign exposure, awareness, knowledge, attitudes, intentions, behavior, and crashes
sources.finding: Identifies measures and their limits and documents the research behind the companion guide. Search initially targeted 2013–2023 US campaigns, then broadened to 1995–2012 and health-communication campaigns when few sources were found. (PDF p. 13)
sources.limits: Not a campaign trial or systematic effectiveness review. Search was a rapid scan (screened result batches until no new relevant sources); toolkit materials were not reviewed by intended SHSO users or subject-matter experts. (PDF pp. 13–14, 40)
sources.access: Official National Academies page; full Web-Only Document 7 PDF, 150 pp.

sources.authors: Phillips, D.; Mohammed, S.; Rantanen, K.; Bury, J.; Sayers, E.; Forsyth, E.; Bertasevicius, V.; Eyers, J.
sources.title: Cycling and Walking Safety: A rapid evidence assessment for the Department for Transport
sources.design: Rapid evidence assessment; narrative synthesis
sources.sample: 114 eligible documents; 51 prioritized for synthesis (24 evidence reviews and 27 quantitative primary studies); 4 synthesized studies addressed road-user education
sources.endpoint: Risk/perceived risk and participation for cycling and walking interventions
sources.finding: Synthesis found only a small, mixed education-campaign evidence base: the randomized Gamble leaflet study changed neither perceived risk nor cycling intention; a THINK! poster pre/post study reported some increased claimed cyclist-safe behaviors; the report concludes evidence is insufficient for firm education-effect conclusions. (PDF pp. 17–18, 36–37; report pp. 14–15, 34–35)
sources.limits: Report cover is dated 17 Sep 2018; GOV.UK publication date is 7 Feb 2020. Single-reviewer screening/data extraction, machine-learning prioritization and synthesis of only 51/114 eligible items limit completeness; only five studies measured both risk and participation. Not a campaign meta-analysis. (PDF pp. 5–7, 12–18; report pp. 3–5, 10–15)
sources.access: Official GOV.UK record and full NatCen report PDF; 80 pp.

sources.authors: Faus, M.; Alonso, F.; Fernández, C.; Useche, S. A.
sources.title: Are Traffic Announcements Really Effective? A Systematic Review of Evaluations of Crash-Prevention Communication Campaigns
sources.design: PRISMA-described systematic mapping/narrative review; no meta-analysis
sources.sample: 27 campaign evaluations selected from 613 records; 24 observational/nonexperimental, 2 experimental, and 1 mixed-method study
sources.endpoint: Attitudes, knowledge, self-reported road-user behavior, and crash outcomes across heterogeneous road-safety campaigns
sources.finding: Reports mixed results: some campaign effects, often temporary; communication tended to perform better alongside legislation or road-safety education. Ten campaigns targeted drink-driving; the review does not establish a cyclist-specific message effect. (PDF pp. 11–14)
sources.limits: Selection involved removing duplicates and inaccessible papers plus manual fit decisions; no reproducible risk-of-bias tool or study-quality ratings are reported in the article. Outcomes and campaigns are highly heterogeneous; co-interventions limit attribution. Do not describe the review as having a formal quality appraisal.
sources.access: Open publisher full text and local candidate PDF; Safety 7(4):66.

sources.authors: Fisa, R.; Musukuma, M.; Sampa, M.; Musonda, P.; Young, T.
sources.title: Effects of interventions for preventing road traffic crashes: an overview of systematic reviews
sources.design: Overview of systematic reviews; descriptive synthesis; AMSTAR 2 appraisal
sources.sample: 35 reviews; five evaluated public-awareness campaigns; 33/35 reviews included studies only from high-income countries
sources.endpoint: Road traffic crashes involving a moving vehicle; awareness campaign findings are not cyclist-specific
sources.finding: The five awareness reviews included three rated critically low quality and two moderate quality. The reported 9% campaign crash reduction is inherited from Phillips et al. (2011), not a new pooled estimate by Fisa et al. (PDF pp. 6, 11, 16)
sources.limits: Excludes crashes without a motor vehicle; evidence is dominated by high-income settings and review quality is generally weak. Fisa’s abstract gives the Phillips campaign interval as −11% to −8%, whereas Phillips et al. report −12% to −6%; use the original Phillips estimate if cited. (PDF pp. 1, 11, 16)
sources.access: Open BMC full text and local candidate PDF; 18 pp.

sources.authors: Stefanidis, K. B.; Davey, B.; Truelove, V.; Schiemer, C.; Freeman, J.
sources.title: Does exposure to social media content influence attitudes towards, and engagement in, road rule violations? A systematic review
sources.design: PRISMA systematic review; qualitative synthesis
sources.sample: 8 English-language peer-reviewed studies; seven content analyses and one focus-group study; searches in four databases to June 2021
sources.endpoint: Social-media road-rule content and its potential relationship to attitudes/behavior; predominantly motor-vehicle driving, not cycling
sources.finding: Review finds risky-driving content online but the evidence cannot establish its effects: the sole exposure/behavior study used focus groups with young men and did not directly measure exposure-related behavior change. (PDF pp. 1, 3, 10–11)
sources.limits: No meta-analysis or risk-of-bias appraisal; excludes grey literature, and the included studies focus on few platforms/topics. Not evidence that cyclist-safety messaging on social media changes behavior. (PDF pp. 2–3, 11)
sources.access: Open PLOS full text and local candidate PDF; 13 pp.

sources.authors: Winters, M.; Weddell, A.; Teschke, K.
sources.title: Is Evidence in Practice? Review of Driver and Cyclist Education Materials with Respect to Cycling Safety Evidence
sources.design: Cycling-safety evidence review paired with a content audit; no intervention evaluation
sources.sample: 56 safety studies and 48 education materials from Canadian driver-licensing jurisdictions, municipalities, and advocacy groups
sources.endpoint: Alignment of cyclist/driver education content with cycling-safety evidence on operations, visibility, road characteristics, routes, and interactions with motor vehicles
sources.finding: Most material topics aligned with the evidence; the authors flagged conflicting guidance about motor-vehicle passing distance/where to ride and a gap in guidance on relative safety of route infrastructure. Useful as a copy-accuracy check, not proof that education changes outcomes. (PDF pp. 1–3; journal pp. 35–38)
sources.limits: Canadian material inventory; one author categorized materials and a subset was checked by another. Safety evidence search used one primary screener, excluded helmet-only studies and subjective safety perceptions, and did not formally critique study methods. (PDF pp. 2–3; journal pp. 36–37)
sources.access: TRB article full text hosted by UBC; TRR 2387, pp. 35–45.

sources.authors: Nachman, E. R.; Rodriguez, D. A.
sources.title: Evaluating the effects of a classroom-based bicycle education intervention on bicycle activity, self-efficacy, personal safety, knowledge, and mode choice
sources.design: Staggered within-person pre/post (case-crossover) panel evaluation of a 2-hour classroom course; not-yet-trained participants supplied same-period comparisons; no random assignment or never-trained control.
sources.sample: 31 classes in nine San Francisco Bay Area cities; current-study survey: 182 baseline, 113 paired; supplemental prior survey: 201 baseline, 45 paired; total 158 paired participants
sources.endpoint: Self-reported bicycling activity, confidence, perceived safety, rules knowledge, and travel mode; Ride Report app used for a small validation subsample
sources.finding: Course participation was associated with higher confidence, car-free-area safety, and rules knowledge; no significant overall change in bicycle trip count. Ride Report agreement check was small (n=12 before; n=11 after removing an outlier), not an objective primary outcome. (PDF pp. 5–8)
sources.limits: Self-selected Bay Area course attendees, substantial follow-up attrition (current sample 40%; supplemental 78%), underpowered relative to target, no control group or crash outcomes; subgroup results exploratory. Training evidence, not a campaign-copy test. (PDF pp. 5, 13–14)
sources.access: Open Frontiers full text and local candidate PDF; 16 pp.

sources.authors: Schönbach, D. M. I.; Altenburg, T. M.; Marques, A.; Chinapaw, M. J. M.; Demetriou, Y.
sources.title: Strategies and effects of school-based interventions to promote active school transportation by bicycle among children and adolescents: a systematic review
sources.design: PRISMA systematic review of controlled trials; narrative synthesis
sources.sample: 9 studies evaluating 7 interventions (2012–2018); ages up to 17; search across 8 databases
sources.endpoint: Active school travel, psychosocial/physical-activity outcomes, and cycling skills; not injury or crash prevention
sources.finding: All nine studies were rated weak quality. Seven favorable outcomes across two studies came from the same adult-guided bicycle-train intervention; overall evidence was judged insufficient, with that program only a promising strategy. (PDF pp. 1–2, 6–9, 14–15)
sources.limits: Highly heterogeneous outcomes precluded meta-analysis; selection bias, blinding, and intervention integrity were weak, contamination common, and adolescent/secondary-school evidence sparse. Not campaign evidence. (PDF pp. 5–6, 14–15)
sources.access: Open BMC full text and local candidate PDF; 17 pp.

sources.authors: Gamble, T.; Walker, I.; Laketa, A.
sources.title: Bicycling campaigns promoting health versus campaigns promoting safety: A randomized controlled online study of ‘dangerization’
sources.design: Randomized online pre/post experiment: safety leaflet, health leaflet, or neutral control
sources.sample: 228 adults recruited opportunistically online; 159 had cycled in prior two weeks and 69 had not
sources.endpoint: Immediate perceived cycling risk, health benefits, enjoyment, and stated intention to cycle
sources.finding: Health leaflet increased non-cyclists’ perceived health benefits; safety leaflet changed neither perceived risk nor health benefits. Neither leaflet changed stated cycling intention or enjoyment. (PDF pp. 3, 10–13)
sources.limits: Immediate post-exposure outcomes measured minutes after one online leaflet; no behavior, participation, or crash endpoint and no check that participants read/understood the leaflet. Convenience sample, self-reports, and a broad cyclist definition limit generalization. Authors’ enjoyment-message suggestion was not tested. (PDF pp. 3, 16–17)
sources.access: Peer-reviewed manuscript full text from University of Bath; published in Journal of Transport & Health 2(3), 369–378.

sources.authors: Sundfør, H. B.; Phillips, R. O.; Aasvik, O.
sources.title: Evaluation of the Norwegian Public Roads Administration’s campaign ‘Most people follow the speed limit’: A norm-based approach to increasing speed compliance
sources.design: Nonrandomized campaign evaluation using repeated nationally representative surveys and objective speed observations
sources.sample: National survey waves and observed speeds across 2019–2025; sample sizes not stated in the one-page English summary; full report is 103 pp in Norwegian
sources.endpoint: Norm perceptions, attitudes, intentions/self-reported speeding, and observed speed-limit compliance
sources.finding: Exposure was most clearly associated with perceived social norms; attitudes improved without a consistent exposure association, and speed observations indicated increased compliance. No control group means effects cannot be causally attributed to the campaign. (English summary, p. 1)
sources.limits: Not cycling-specific; local English full text is only a one-page summary, so samples, analyses, and estimates could not be independently checked here. Official TØI page links the full Norwegian report.
sources.access: Official TØI publication page, English summary PDF, and linked Norwegian report.

sources.authors: Tyagi, S.; Wragg, N.; Suhendra, F.
sources.title: That resonated with me: A user-centred approach to understanding young adult vulnerable road users’ road safety campaigns messaging needs—Case study
sources.design: Qualitative user-centered case study using workshops
sources.sample: 30 young adult vulnerable road users in Australia; workshop participants
sources.endpoint: Audience interpretation and preferences for campaign messages
sources.finding: Participants described value in specific, purposeful, actionable instructions and highlighted multiple road-user roles and intersectional identities.
sources.limits: Qualitative formative findings are not a test of message effects on driving, riding, crashes, or injuries. Transfer to other age groups or settings needs testing.
sources.access: Open publisher article page and indexed abstract; no local full-text PDF obtained.

sources.authors: Limb, M.; Collyer, S.
sources.title: The effect of safety attire on perceptions of cyclist dehumanisation
sources.design: Self-selected online image-perception experiment with paired forced-choice photographs
sources.sample: 563 survey respondents in Australia; nonrepresentative convenience sample
sources.endpoint: Ratings or choices of perceived cyclist humanity in photographs
sources.finding: Photographs of cyclists in helmets or safety vests were more likely to be selected as less human than photographs without safety attire.
sources.limits: Perception ratings are not observed driver behavior or injury; self-selected sample limits generalization. Do not infer that riders should avoid protective equipment.
sources.access: Full article PDF in research collection; indexed journal record.

sources.authors: Torres-Barragán, C. A.; Cottrill, C. D.; Beecroft, M.
sources.title: Spatial inequalities and media representation of cycling safety in Bogotá, Colombia
sources.design: Spatial and archival case study of local crash reporting, infrastructure, and socioeconomic patterns
sources.sample: Bogotá newspaper accounts of cyclist deaths/injuries, 2002–2017
sources.endpoint: Place and media representation of cyclist harm
sources.finding: Reports and safety conditions were uneven across places and social groups, motivating attention to whose risks and experiences a campaign represents.
sources.limits: Single-city observational case study; newspaper coverage is an incomplete crash source and no message intervention was tested.
sources.access: Open publisher full article page and indexed TRID record.

sources.authors: Ferenchak, N. N.; Sanchez Rodriguez, O.; Losada-Rojas, L. L.; Schneider, R.; Gu, X.
sources.title: Longitudinal socioeconomic and built environment shifts in US bicyclist fatality locations 2001–2020
sources.design: Longitudinal census-tract analysis of U.S. bicyclist fatalities and neighborhood context
sources.sample: FARS fatality locations, 2001–2020; census and EPA spatial variables
sources.endpoint: Area-level fatality locations and correlates
sources.finding: Fatality locations shifted toward lower-density areas; tracts with fatalities had distinct socioeconomic characteristics relative to national averages.
sources.limits: Area-level associations are not individual risk estimates or message effects; commute data imperfectly measures bicycling exposure and road speed/volume were unavailable nationally.
sources.access: Open publisher full article under Creative Commons license.

sources.authors: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
sources.title: Communicating Safe Behavior Practices to Vulnerable Road Users
sources.design: BTSCRP Web-Only Document 6; practitioner toolkit and planning guidance
sources.sample: 192-page report; not an intervention sample
sources.endpoint: Audience, channel, and campaign design methods for vulnerable road users
sources.finding: Provides tools for identifying safety problems, audience needs, feasible behavioral targets, and communication channels.
sources.limits: Guidance and component examples do not establish that any particular print message reduces cyclist crashes or injuries.
sources.access: Official National Academies online full text; PDF download requires guest or account access.

sources.authors: Høye, A.; Fyhri, A.; Bjørnskau, T.
sources.title: Shared road is double happiness: Evaluation of a Share the Road sign
sources.design: Before/after roadside surveys on a test road and a comparison road near Oslo
sources.sample: Cyclists and car drivers recruited on two roads
sources.endpoint: Self-reported and perceived behaviors; sign awareness
sources.finding: Reported passing behavior improved on the test road relative to comparison road
sources.limits: Season and respondent composition varied; primarily recreational traffic; outcomes were reported behavior, not measured passing distance
sources.access: Full author manuscript in local research collection

sources.authors: Dalton, A.; Sumner, F.; Jones, A.
sources.title: Digital screen use for a road safety campaign message was not associated with attitudes or knowledge of passers-by: an experimental study
sources.design: Quasi-experiment comparing control and screen-exposure days
sources.sample: 364 public interview respondents over five days
sources.endpoint: Reported message awareness, recall and attitudes
sources.finding: 364 interviews over five days; image displayed on two intervention days. No significant intervention-day difference in priority ranking or recall of the numeric claim. Survey outcomes after brief exposure, not driving or injuries.
sources.limits: Short exposure and survey responses; no direct observation of driving behavior
sources.access: University repository abstract and author accepted manuscript

sources.authors: Bacchieri, G.; Barros, A. J. D.; dos Santos, J. V.; Gonçalves, H.; Gigante, D. P.
sources.title: A community intervention to prevent traffic accidents among bicycle commuters
sources.design: Stepped-wedge community intervention with monthly telephone follow-up
sources.sample: 1133 adult male bicycle commuters in Pelotas, Brazil
sources.endpoint: Self-reported traffic crashes and near-crashes per cyclist-month
sources.finding: After adjusting for time the study found no statistically significant protective effect on crashes or near-crashes
sources.limits: Approximately 45% did not attend; self-report; combined educational, equipment and brake-check package; context and secular trends affect interpretation
sources.access: Full original journal article PDF

sources.authors: Houts, P. S.; Doak, C. C.; Doak, L. G.; Loscalzo, M. J.
sources.title: The role of pictures in improving health communication: A review of research on attention, comprehension, recall, and adherence
sources.design: Narrative review of health-communication, psychology, education and marketing research
sources.sample: Varied populations and interventions
sources.endpoint: Attention, comprehension, recall and adherence
sources.finding: Pictures closely paired with text can support attention, recall and comprehension; spatial and relational diagrams can help understanding
sources.limits: Indirect for cycling; heterogeneous interventions and outcomes; narrative review, not a cycling-campaign effect estimate
sources.access: Full published article PDF from University of Trieste repository; sections 4 and 8 checked

sources.authors: Calderón, R.; Sheveland, A.; Outman, M.; Sharma, A.
sources.title: A Nationwide Review of Pedestrian and Bicyclist Safety Education in Driver Education
sources.design: Structured content audit of driver-education resources
sources.sample: Methods pp. 3-4: 31 curriculum guides across 30 states; 50 manuals (49 states and DC); 11 training resources. Discussion p. 27 instead gives 49 manuals and 13 trainings.
sources.endpoint: Coverage of pedestrian and bicyclist safety topics in education materials
sources.finding: Coverage varied. Manuals emphasized rules over safe-driving practices; many training resources omitted newer facilities such as bike boxes. Use to identify local teaching gaps.
sources.limits: Content audit, not an intervention trial. Methods and discussion disagree on manual/training counts; narrative report omits totals. No estimate of changes in driving or injuries.
sources.access: Full original NHTSA report DOT HS 813 655; local copy from Pedestrian and Bicycle Information Center; methods pp. 3-4 and discussion pp. 27-28 checked

figures.title: Rewrite the prompt.
figures.caption: Figure 1. Rewrite the prompt. Name the situation and action. Use the action-focused version as a draft, then ask drivers to explain when they should wait.
figures.alt: A vague share-the-road prompt is rewritten as a driver instruction to slow down and wait when there is no safe passing room.
figures.topic: Why a message might work

figures.title: Match support to the barrier.
figures.caption: Figure 2. Match support to the barrier. Ask the audience what gets in the way; barriers may overlap. The examples illustrate a planning approach, so test the response locally.
figures.alt: Four separate examples connect rule knowledge, riding skills, equipment access and road conditions to the support each needs.
figures.topic: Why a message might work

figures.title: Show why waiting is the right choice.
figures.caption: Figure 3. Show why waiting is the right choice. This schematic depicts a waiting position. In your own material, show the local road context and the space needed for a lawful, safe pass.
figures.alt: A labeled top-down road scene shows oncoming traffic, a rider avoiding a rough edge, and a driver waiting behind because there is no safe passing space.
figures.topic: Passing and lane position: clarity with behavioral follow-through

figures.title: Make waiting the obvious next step.
figures.caption: Print example 1. Make waiting the obvious next step. Use a specific action and a scene the audience can explain. The sign-comprehension study informs the clear instruction; the new artwork and wording are illustrative. Test the road scene and the meaning of waiting. R15, R67.
figures.alt: A purple and yellow driver poster shows a car waiting behind a cyclist on a narrow road with opposing traffic.
figures.topic: Passing and lane position: clarity with behavioral follow-through

figures.title: Make the door check a sequence.
figures.caption: Figure 4. Make the door check a sequence. Put the check before the open door. Using the far hand can prompt a turn to look behind; adapt the check to the person and vehicle. Ask viewers when the door must stay closed.
figures.alt: Three panels show a parked car, a driver looking back toward a bicycle while the door stays closed, waiting for the bicycle to pass, then opening only when clear.
figures.topic: Doors, junctions and large vehicles

figures.title: Turn advice into a short sequence.
figures.caption: Print example 2. Turn advice into a short sequence. Pair the card with a parked-vehicle demonstration. R06 examined how drivers understood door-opening reminders; R09 examined head movements during a door check. Ask the reader to explain and demonstrate the sequence. R06, R09.
figures.alt: A four-by-six-inch reminder card uses three numbered steps: check with the door closed, wait for approaching traffic, and open when clear.
figures.topic: Doors, junctions and large vehicles

figures.title: Show the turning driver waiting.
figures.caption: Figure 5. Show the turning driver waiting. Redraw this example for the actual traffic direction, signals and road layout. For large vehicles, use vehicle-specific visibility information rather than a generic blind-spot outline.
figures.alt: A right-side-driving schematic labels the driver waiting before a turn crosses the bicycle path, with a dashed intended-turn route, solid rider direction, badge 1 at the crossing and badge 2 beside the waiting car.
figures.topic: Doors, junctions and large vehicles

figures.title: Give the turning driver a clear job.
figures.caption: Print example 3. Give the turning driver a clear job. Use an actual local layout in the final design and teach the vehicle-specific visibility check. The illustration applies the safety guidance discussed in this chapter. R45.
figures.alt: An A5 driver poster says Check, then wait and shows an intended turn crossing a bicycle path while the driver stays behind.
figures.topic: Doors, junctions and large vehicles

figures.title: Pair a backstory with the driver action.
figures.caption: Figure 6. Pair a backstory with the driver action. The fictional story gives an everyday ride a personal context. The person is AI-generated and the story is invented; test this draft with the intended audience.
figures.alt: AI-generated illustration of a person beside a bicycle with the fictional story Maya is riding home after visiting a friend and the instruction No safe room to pass? Slow down and wait.
figures.topic: Human stories, identity and blame

figures.title: Check whether the response lasts.
figures.caption: Figure 7. Check whether the response lasts. The two video studies covered cyclists and horse riders. This timeline summarizes assessment points, not the size or shape of change between them. Plan a later check of your own campaign; the follow-up did not test a repeat-message schedule. Sources: R07-R08, cited above.
figures.alt: A timeline distinguishes baseline, immediate attitude and passing-intention improvements, and a sixteen-month follow-up where those benefits were not detected versus baseline.
figures.topic: Human stories, identity and blame

figures.title: Vary the story, keep the safe action.
figures.caption: Figure 8. Vary the story, keep the safe action. Try everyday roles that fit the community. Check whether the story helps viewers recognize the person and remember the driver action.
figures.alt: Three sample message cards use mother, teacher and friend roles while keeping the same passing instruction.
figures.topic: Human stories, identity and blame

figures.title: Pair a human connection with a safe action.
figures.caption: Print example 4. Pair a human connection with a safe action. The relationship headline is a creative hypothesis to test. The cited studies examined responses to photographs and videos. Check whether readers connect with the portrait and can name the driver action. R31, R07, R08.
figures.alt: A portrait poster pairs A friend, riding home with a prominent instruction to slow down and wait behind when there is no safe passing room.
figures.topic: Human stories, identity and blame

figures.title: Turn emotion into a usable action.
figures.caption: Figure 9. Turn emotion into a usable action. Ask viewers what they would do next and whether the message makes riding feel more or less welcoming.
figures.alt: A consequence-only message is compared with an action-focused turning instruction.
figures.topic: Fear, social norms and creative style

figures.title: Replace alarm with a usable action.
figures.caption: Print example 5. Replace alarm with a usable action. Use the pair to find out what readers understand and feel. Fear-appeal evidence motivates checking both the intended response and possible harm. Use the explanations to improve the draft. R35, R28.
figures.alt: Two A5 posters use the same turning scene: one presents a consequence-only headline, the other gives a check-and-wait instruction.
figures.topic: Fear, social norms and creative style

figures.title: Choose a truthful claim.
figures.caption: Figure 10. Choose a truthful claim. Check the source, population and timing before using a norm. If the data are missing, use a clear action and test its meaning.
figures.alt: Two paths show that a norm claim needs actual local data and a source, while a clear passing instruction can be used without inventing a statistic.
figures.topic: Fear, social norms and creative style

figures.title: Use an instruction when local data are absent.
figures.caption: Print example 6. Use an instruction when local data are absent. This illustrates the choice discussed in the norms section: use an accurate instruction when no relevant local behavior statistic is available. Test the meaning of each step. R30, R03.
figures.alt: A bright yellow door-check poster uses Pause, look, open when clear without an unsupported claim about what most people do.
figures.topic: Fear, social norms and creative style

figures.title: Build the card around the lesson.
figures.caption: Figure 11. Build the card around the lesson. Show the skill taught, the safe place to practice, and where to get feedback. A take-home reminder can point to the next session.
figures.alt: Three panels use rider and instructor icons to show a demonstration, supervised practice and feedback in a closed area, with a later skill check.
figures.topic: Rider education and supervised practice

figures.title: Make a handout part of a real lesson.
figures.caption: Print example 7. Make a handout part of a real lesson. Distribute the card through an existing supervised program. The studies support assessing specific skills and follow-up; the card is an example of connecting print to that work. R05, R38, R55.
figures.alt: A take-home learner card says Build the skill before the traffic and asks the learner to agree on the next practice step with an instructor.
figures.topic: Rider education and supervised practice

figures.title: Show the conditions that matter.
figures.caption: Figure 12. Show the conditions that matter. These are mechanism illustrations based on the mixed pedestrian/cyclist detection literature, not measured brightness or injury effects. Demonstrate the actual equipment in relevant conditions. Source: Kwan and Mapstone, R20, cited above.
figures.alt: Daylight and night-time panels illustrate fluorescent clothing in daylight and retroreflective material in headlights after dark; the night panel shows light reaching and returning from a reflective strip.
figures.topic: Lights, visibility and helmets: separate advice, access and effect

figures.title: Explain an uncertain estimate visually.
figures.caption: Figure 13. Explain an uncertain estimate visually. The dot is the estimate and the line is its 95% confidence interval for injury crashes involving another road user. A ratio of 1 means equal rates. The wide interval spans lower and higher rates; it is not a guaranteed range for an individual rider. Source: Hels et al. (2025), Table 9, R42.
figures.alt: A linear rate-ratio chart shows the corrected estimate 0.75 and its 95 percent confidence interval from 0.23 to 2.47, spanning the reference value of one.
figures.topic: Lights, visibility and helmets: separate advice, access and effect

figures.title: Make equipment advice visible.
figures.caption: Figure 14. Make equipment advice visible. Photograph or illustrate the actual mounts you teach. Pair the guide with fitting help, and check that riders can perform the steps.
figures.alt: A bicycle illustration identifies front and rear lights alongside fit, aim, switch-on and battery checks, with a prompt to ask for fitting help.
figures.topic: Lights, visibility and helmets: separate advice, access and effect

figures.title: Put a checklist beside the equipment.
figures.caption: Print example 8. Put a checklist beside the equipment. Use this as a prompt during fitting, then replace the schematic with the actual equipment. The visibility evidence concerns seeing equipment under specific conditions. Demonstrate the checks with the actual lights and fitting instructions. R20, R67.
figures.alt: A five-by-seven-inch counter sign shows front and rear bicycle lights and four checks: mounts, power, switching on and aiming.
figures.topic: Lights, visibility and helmets: separate advice, access and effect

figures.title: Advertise help people can use.
figures.caption: Figure 15. Advertise help people can use. A fitting invitation connects a reminder to a service. Confirm staff capacity, equipment access and the way participants will obtain help.
figures.alt: A rider and trained helper stand at a table with a helmet, beside an invitation to get fitting help and a reminder to confirm service capacity.
figures.topic: Lights, visibility and helmets: separate advice, access and effect

figures.title: Plan the route to the audience.
figures.caption: Figure 16. Plan the route to the audience. Choose a setting people already use, name the partner, and record what help is delivered. Review reach among people outside existing cycling groups.
figures.alt: Three delivery examples connect fleet drivers, parents and riders, and people needing lights with a stationary setting and supporting partner.
figures.topic: Campaigns inside larger safety programs

figures.title: Make every element earn its space.
figures.caption: Figure 17. Make every element earn its space. Use this structure to review a draft: can viewers find the situation and action before being distracted by the image or brand? This is an illustrative 3fp.org layout; use your own organization and a relevant destination when adapting it.
figures.alt: An annotated sample poster identifies four jobs: a relatable image, a named situation, a clear driver action, and a short web address.
figures.topic: A practical brief for organizations and creative teams

figures.title: Compare two image choices.
figures.caption: Figure 18. Compare two image choices. These AI-generated images illustrate two visual directions. Match the subject, crop, wording and layout, note any remaining differences, and ask the same questions of both versions.
figures.alt: Two sample poster layouts use AI-generated photo-style and illustrated versions of the same portrait beside identical passing instructions. Ask who should act and what happens next.
figures.topic: A practical brief for organizations and creative teams

figures.title: Check the real format.
figures.caption: Figure 19. Check the real format. Print a sample at its intended size, test each translation, and ask users to explain the next action. Give people a working way to get help.
figures.alt: Print, language and access panels show clear type, community-reviewed adaptation and alternatives to QR-only access, with a teach-back prompt.
figures.topic: A practical brief for organizations and creative teams

figures.title: Match measures to the campaign.
figures.caption: Figure 20. Match measures to the campaign. Choose measures that fit the goal and resources. The sequence is a planning model, and each step needs its own evidence.
figures.alt: Five campaign measures: reach, understanding, opportunity, behavior and safety. Check access and unintended harm across the people served.
figures.topic: Evaluate what the campaign is supposed to change

figures.title: Measure change against a comparison.
figures.caption: Figure 21. Measure change against a comparison. The diagram illustrates a controlled before/after design, with no invented results. An evaluation partner should consider differences between groups, how groups are chosen, whether the comparison group also sees the campaign, and other changes over time. Use the evaluation guidance cited in this section to choose a design that fits the campaign.
figures.alt: A two-row timeline shows the campaign and comparison groups measured before and after, with the campaign and support introduced only in the campaign group.
figures.topic: Evaluate what the campaign is supposed to change

figures.title: Report a small pretest clearly.
figures.caption: Figure 22. Report a small pretest clearly. The counts in this example are invented for teaching. Use your actual counts, recruitment and question, then explain what you changed and what you will test next.
figures.alt: An invented comparison shows 6 of 10 people understanding version A and 9 of 10 understanding version B, with wording that reports a small early test accurately.
figures.topic: Evaluate what the campaign is supposed to change

figures.title: Take the plan to your partners.
figures.caption: Figure 23. Take the plan to your partners. Assign an owner, timing and resources to each step. Use the findings from one run to improve the next.
figures.alt: A numbered loop runs from encounter to support, drafting, pretesting, delivery, and measurement, then back to the next planning cycle.
figures.topic: What to do, what to avoid, what to study next

quickGuide.title: Make a safety message people can use
quickGuide.banner: Put safer streets first. Work for safer road design and speeds. Use your campaign to explain road changes and help people take a safe action now.

steps.title: Pick one audience and one moment
steps.body: Choose a specific situation, such as a driver passing on a narrow road. Ask what makes the safe action hard: an unclear rule, a missing skill, the cost of gear, or the road itself.

steps.title: Say exactly what to do
steps.body: Name the moment and give a clear action. Put that instruction in the headline. Use plain words. Keep your logo and extra information smaller than the safety message.

steps.title: Show the action in the picture
steps.body: Show a driver waiting, a door staying closed, or a light being fitted. Put a short explanation beside the action. If you use a portrait or story, keep the safety instruction easy to find.

steps.title: Pair advice with practical help
steps.body: Pair light advice with gear and fitting help; pair skill advice with instruction, practice and feedback. Confirm the help exists. Say where to get it, what it costs and who can use it.

steps.title: Reach people in familiar places
steps.body: Work with driving schools, employers, bike shops, schools and local groups. Use places where people can stop and read. Choose languages and formats with the people you need to reach.

steps.title: Ask people before you print a large batch
steps.body: Show a draft to a few people from your audience. Ask these questions before you explain the message. Write down the answers and revise anything that causes confusion or blame.

steps.title: Check the finished piece
steps.body: Print a sample at its real size. Make the main action easy to read. Ask a local safety expert to check the road scene and rules. Ask local speakers to check each translation. Test the QR code and include a short web address too.

steps.title: Check what people learn and use
steps.body: Record where you shared the material and how many people took part. Ask readers to explain the action. For a lesson or gear check, ask people to show the skill or check the equipment later. Use what you learn to improve the next version.

examples.label: PASSING
examples.text: No safe room to pass? Slow down and wait behind.

examples.label: DOORS
examples.text: Keep the door closed. Look beside and behind. Open only when clear.

examples.label: TURNING
examples.text: Before turning across a rider’s path, check and wait until the rider has cleared.

questions: What, if anything, is confusing or unfair?
quickGuide.test_tip: Compare one change at a time. To test a picture, keep the words and layout the same. Use small tests to find problems, then revise and check again.
